title: Node vs Python vs Go for AI Backends (2026)
summary:
An AI feature is roughly half model prompts and half boring backend work: auth, rate limits, queues, webhooks, and cost control. That is why the stack question — Node/Express, Python, or Go for an AI backend in 2026 — comes up on day one.

Short answer up front: Python for heavy AI/RAG experimentation, Node when your product is already JavaScript/TypeScript, Go when you need ultra-efficient service glue at scale — not as your first LangChain tutorial language.

I am Vishvajeet Shukla, a full-stack developer working across Next.js, Node, and AI integrations. Related: LangChain RAG website agent · developer blog.

Decision table (2026 practical view)

Need Best default Why
LangChain / notebooks / research pace Python Ecosystem depth
Next.js site chatbot on same repo Node / TS One language, simple deploy
High QPS gateway, low memory Go Efficient concurrency
Fast MVP for client demo Node or Python Whichever your team ships faster
ML training pipelines Python Not even a contest

Node.js + Express (or Next.js route handlers)

Strengths

  • Same language as React/Next frontends
  • Great for streaming responses to the browser
  • LangChain.js, Vercel AI SDK, OpenAI official SDKs are solid
  • Easy JSON APIs, middleware, auth patterns for web apps

Watch-outs

  • CPU-heavy embedding of huge corpora can block the event loop if you do it naively
  • Move bulk ingest to workers/queues

Use Node when: your portfolio or SaaS is already TS, and the agent is a product feature not a research lab.

Python (FastAPI / Django Ninja / Flask)

Strengths

  • LangChain, LlamaIndex, eval tools, notebooks everywhere
  • Fastest path to try retrieval strategies
  • Data cleaning and PDF parsing ecosystem

Watch-outs

  • Extra service to deploy if the main app is Node
  • You must still design production concerns (timeouts, workers, observability)

Use Python when: RAG quality and iteration speed matter more than monorepo purity.

Go

Strengths

  • Simple concurrency model, small binaries, predictable performance
  • Excellent for API gateways, rate limiters, fan-out proxies

Watch-outs

  • AI orchestration libraries and examples lag Python/JS
  • You will call model HTTP APIs yourself more often

Use Go when: you already know Go and need a thin, fast control plane — not when learning RAG for the first time.

LangChain workflow: which language?

  • Learning RAG + agents quickly → Python
  • Shipping on a Next.js portfolio with existing API routes → Node/TS (LangChain.js)
  • Hardening a multi-tenant gateway later → maybe Go in front of either

Full agent pattern: LangChain RAG for website AI agents.

Architecture patterns that beat language debates

  1. Sync API for short chat turns
  2. Queue + worker for re-indexing site content
  3. Stream tokens to UI for perceived speed
  4. Cache frequent answers
  5. Separate secrets from the frontend bundle

Language does not fix a missing rate limiter.

Performance and cost realities

  • Model tokens dominate cost more than language runtime for most MVPs
  • Retrieval quality dominates answer quality more than framework brand
  • Cold starts matter on serverless — warm workers help long RAG chains

Team and hiring angle (India freelancing reality)

  • More full-stack freelancers are comfortable in JS/TS
  • AI/ML specialists lean Python
  • Go talent is excellent but smaller pool for AI-feature MVPs

Ship with the language your maintainer can debug at 11pm.

Recommended defaults by project type

Project Backend pick
Portfolio chat over blogs Node (Next API) + vector DB
Document-heavy enterprise RAG Python worker + any web API
WhatsApp AI session service Node or Python + Redis
Multi-tenant AI gateway at scale Go edge + Python/Node workers

Express server sketch (when Node is right) 

// conceptual only
app.post('/api/chat', rateLimit, auth, async (req, res) => {
  const chunks = await retrieve(req.body.question)
  const answer = await generate({ question, chunks })
  res.json({ answer, sources: chunks.map(c => c.url) })
})

Add streaming, timeouts, and abuse controls before public launch.

Python FastAPI sketch (when Python is right) 

# conceptual only
@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(q: Query):
    chunks = await retrieve(q.text)
    answer = await generate(q.text, chunks)
    return {"answer": answer, "sources": [c.url for c in chunks]}

My personal recommendation for most website agents

If the product is a Next.js site (like many modern portfolios and SaaS marketing apps): start with TypeScript + LangChain.js or Vercel AI SDK. Spin a Python service only when ingest/eval complexity outgrows the JS tooling.

Reach for Go when traffic and infrastructure concerns dominate, not when you are still writing the first system prompt.

SEO/AdSense note for developer blogs

Comparison posts like this earn developer traffic when they stay practical and updated. Keep examples honest, avoid fake benchmarks, and link to deeper tutorials. That is also the AdSense-safe way: real teaching, not scraped listicles.

FAQ

Is Express outdated for AI APIs?

No. Express (or Fastify) is still fine. Next.js route handlers are also fine. Structure and ops matter more than the framework logo.

Is Python slower than Go for chat APIs?

For typical LLM calls, network and model latency dominate. Language microbenchmarks rarely decide UX.

Can I mix all three?

Yes — many mature systems do. Start with one to reduce ops pain.

What about Rust?

Great for specialised high-performance components. Overkill for most first AI agents.

What should freelancers learn first?

If you sell web apps: TypeScript + one RAG path. Add Python when clients need heavier data workflows.

title: Why Positive Grid Profit Can Coexist With Negative Total P&L
summary:
A grid-bot dashboard can show profitable completed cycles while the overall account is losing money. These figures describe different parts of the strategy. For anyone building a trading dashboard, preserving that distinction is an accounting requirement.

Separate completed cycles from open exposure

Grid profit summarizes completed buy/sell cycles according to the platform's reporting rules. Total P&L also depends on open positions and the costs assigned to the account. Read the venue's definitions before combining its fields: a fee already included in a reported profit must not be subtracted again.

Consider an explicitly hypothetical example:

Component Illustrative units
Completed-cycle profit +20
Open-position P&L -35
Additional costs not yet counted above -3
Total -18

The positive cycle result does not cover the open loss and remaining costs. This is an accounting illustration, not a backtest or a claim about a real bot.

Make the accounting boundary explicit in code

A small pure function can express the example, provided every input uses the same currency, time window and accounting boundary:

from decimal import Decimal

def illustrative_total(cycle_profit, open_pnl, extra_costs):
    # extra_costs is positive for costs, and excludes costs
    # already included in either of the first two inputs.
    return cycle_profit + open_pnl - extra_costs

result = illustrative_total(
    Decimal('20'), Decimal('-35'), Decimal('3')
)
# result == Decimal('-18')

This is not a universal exchange reconciliation function. Real adapters must separately handle deposits, withdrawals, realized position P&L, funding and the exact definition of each venue field. Decimal arithmetic avoids binary floating-point surprises, but it cannot fix incorrectly classified inputs.

Four questions for a dashboard

  1. Is the result live, backtested or simulated?
  2. What time window and starting capital does it cover?
  3. Which fees, funding and capital flows are included?
  4. Can another reader reproduce the inputs and assumptions?

For a platform-specific example of the distinction, see Bybit's Spot Grid Bot FAQ. Spot and futures accounting should not be treated as interchangeable.

title: Will It Fit? Turn a Laptop's Screen Size into Real Dimensions with Python
summary:
"Fits 15.6-inch laptops" is printed on a lot of backpacks, but 15.6 inches is the screen diagonal, not the size of the machine. A bit of Pythagoras turns the diagonal into width and height.

Screen size from diagonal and aspect ratio

For a ratio of w:h, the diagonal is the hypotenuse, so each side is a share of it:

from math import hypot

def screen_mm(diag_in, ratio=(16, 9)):
    rw, rh = ratio
    k = diag_in * 25.4 / hypot(rw, rh)
    return round(rw * k), round(rh * k)

for d, r in [(14, (16, 9)), (15.6, (16, 9)), (16, (16, 10)), (17.3, (16, 9))]:
    print(d, r, screen_mm(d, r))

14 (16, 9) (310, 174)
15.6 (16, 9) (345, 194)
16 (16, 10) (345, 215)
17.3 (16, 9) (383, 215)

Notice that a 16-inch 16:10 screen is as wide as a 15.6-inch 16:9 one, just taller.

From screen to body

The body adds bezels, plus a deeper bottom edge for the hinge. The allowances below are rough guesses, so replace them with your laptop's spec sheet when you have it:

def body_estimate(diag_in, ratio=(16, 9), side=12, top=12, bottom=40):
    w, h = screen_mm(diag_in, ratio)
    return w + 2 * side, h + top + bottom

print(body_estimate(15.6))  # (369, 246)

Checking a sleeve 

def fits(laptop_mm, sleeve_mm, margin=10):
    return all(s >= l + margin for l, s in zip(laptop_mm, sleeve_mm))

Measure the sleeve inside, flat, and allow a few millimetres for the padding.

PackForge's bulk laptop backpacks (about 20 to 30 litres) have a padded compartment for 15.6-inch laptops, with 17-inch versions made to order and logo branding available: Laptop backpacks.

title: Noise Exposure Math for Factory Floors: A Small Python Helper
summary:
Compressors, presses, looms and DG sets can push a shop floor well past safe noise levels. Here is a small Python helper to estimate how long people can stay in an area and how much hearing protection helps.

Allowed time at a given level

The NIOSH recommended limit is 85 dBA for 8 hours, with a 3 dB exchange rate: every 3 dB more halves the allowed time.

def allowed_hours(dba, limit=85, exchange=3):
    return 8 / 2 ** ((dba - limit) / exchange)

for level in (85, 88, 91, 94, 100):
    print(level, "dBA ->", round(allowed_hours(level), 2), "h")

85 dBA -> 8.0 h
88 dBA -> 4.0 h
91 dBA -> 2.0 h
94 dBA -> 1.0 h
100 dBA -> 0.25 h

Daily noise dose

Most people move between areas during a shift. The dose adds up each part: hours spent divided by hours allowed at that level. Over 100% means too much.

def daily_dose(exposures):  # list of (dBA, hours)
    return 100 * sum(h / allowed_hours(l) for l, h in exposures)

shift = [(92, 2), (86, 4), (80, 2)]
print(round(daily_dose(shift)), "%")  # 197 %

Estimating protection

The NRR on a label is measured in a lab, so NIOSH suggests derating it: 25% off for earmuffs, 50% for foam plugs and 70% for other plugs, then subtracting 7 dB when you work in dBA.

DERATE = {"earmuff": 0.25, "foam_plug": 0.50, "other_plug": 0.70}

def protected_level(dba, nrr, kind):
    effective = nrr * (1 - DERATE[kind]) - 7
    return dba - max(effective, 0)

print(protected_level(95, 27, "earmuff"))  # 81.75

Caveats

Rules differ by country (OSHA, for example, uses 90 dBA with a 5 dB exchange rate), so use your local limits. Measure real levels with a sound level meter, and use the rating printed on the protector you actually buy. This is a planning tool, not a substitute for a proper noise survey.

title: GSM to Kilograms: Work Out Copier Paper Weight per Ream in Python
summary:
Ordering paper for an office is easier when you know what a carton weighs before it arrives. The GSM printed on the ream (grams per square metre) is all you need to work it out.

The formula

weight of one sheet = GSM x sheet area (m²)

A4 is 210 x 297 mm, so one sheet is 0.21 x 0.297 = 0.06237 m². A3 is exactly twice that.

SIZES_M2 = {"A4": 0.210 * 0.297, "A3": 0.297 * 0.420}

def ream_kg(gsm, size="A4", sheets=500):
    return gsm * SIZES_M2[size] * sheets / 1000

for gsm in (70, 75, 80):
    print(gsm, "GSM A4 ream:", round(ream_kg(gsm), 2), "kg")

Output:

70 GSM A4 ream: 2.18 kg
75 GSM A4 ream: 2.34 kg
80 GSM A4 ream: 2.49 kg

An 80 GSM A3 ream comes to about 4.99 kg.

Cartons

Paper usually ships in cartons of 5 or 10 reams:

def carton_kg(gsm, reams, size="A4"):
    return ream_kg(gsm, size) * reams

print(round(carton_kg(80, 5), 1))   # 12.5
print(round(carton_kg(80, 10), 1))  # 24.9

That is paper only; the carton itself adds a little more.

How many reams a month? 

def reams_per_month(pages_per_day, working_days=26):
    return pages_per_day * working_days / 500

title: MCP Token Cost: I Cut My MCP Server From 15 Tools to 4
summary:
MCP Token Cost: I Cut My MCP Server From 15 Tools to 4

Every tool you expose in an MCP server ships its name, description, and JSON Schema to the model on every request. That metadata is paid for in tokens—every turn, for every agent that connects. I had 15 tools in a file-management MCP server. My system prompt was 4,800 tokens before the user said a word. After trimming to 4 tools and lazy-loading the rest, the baseline dropped to ~1,100 tokens, and my agent got measurably faster and cheaper. Here is the problem, the solution, and the code.

The Problem: Tool Metadata Is a Fixed Tax

MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers advertise capabilities via tools/list. Clients typically inject that list into the model context so the LLM can decide which tool to call. The cost isn't the tool call—it's the advertisement. A typical tool looks like this:

{
  "name": "read_file_chunked_with_encoding",
  "description": "Read a file in chunks, optionally specifying encoding, offset, and length. Supports UTF-8, UTF-16, latin-1...",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "path": {"type": "string", "description": "Absolute path to the file"},
      "encoding": {"type": "string", "enum": ["utf-8", "utf-16", "latin-1"]},
      "offset": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
      "length": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1}
    },
    "required": ["path"]
  }
}

That's roughly 120–180 tokens. Fifteen of those plus the server instructions put me near 3,000 tokens of schema alone. Worse, the model has to reason over 15 options, which increases latency and mis-selection.

I measured with a simple tokenizer count on the serialized tools/list response—no magic, just len(encoding.encode(json.dumps(tools))) using tiktoken.

The Solution: Fewer, Coarser Tools + a Discovery Tool

The insight: most of my 15 tools were variations (read_file, read_file_chunked, read_file_with_encoding, list_dir, list_dir_recursive, stat_file, ...). Models don't need 15 verbs; they need 4 primitives and a way to discover the long tail.

My final surface:

  1. fs_read – read a file (path, optional offset/limit)
  2. fs_write – write or append to a file
  3. fs_list – list a directory (non-recursive; recursion via repeated calls)
  4. fs_search – search file contents with a regex

Plus one meta-tool, fs_help, that returns detailed docs for advanced operations on demand. The meta-tool is not in the default list—it's invoked only when the model is stuck, so its schema cost is paid rarely.

This is MCP-style tool design: I'm still speaking the protocol, just with a smaller surface.

Implementation

1. A minimal MCP-style server (stdio JSON-RPC)

Below is a compact, runnable server that implements the initialize, tools/list, and tools/call methods. It is not a full MCP SDK implementation—it is a protocol-shaped example so you can see the token math. For production, use the official mcp Python SDK.

import json, sys, re, os
from pathlib import Path

BASE = Path(os.environ.get("MCP_ROOT", ".")).resolve()

def safe_path(p: str) -> Path:
    target = (BASE / p).resolve()
    if not str(target).startswith(str(BASE)):
        raise ValueError("path escapes root")
    return target

TOOLS = [
    {
        "name": "fs_read",
        "description": "Read a UTF-8 text file. Optional offset/limit are line numbers.",
        "inputSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "path": {"type": "string"},
                "offset": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
                "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1},
            },
            "required": ["path"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "fs_write",
        "description": "Write text to a file. Set append=true to append.",
        "inputSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "path": {"type": "string"},
                "content": {"type": "string"},
                "append": {"type": "boolean", "default": False},
            },
            "required": ["path", "content"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "fs_list",
        "description": "List entries in a directory (non-recursive).",
        "inputSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"path": {"type": "string", "default": "."}},
            "required": [],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "fs_search",
        "description": "Search file contents under a directory using a Python regex.",
        "inputSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "path": {"type": "string", "default": "."},
                "pattern": {"type": "string"},
                "max_results": {"type": "integer", "default": 50},
            },
            "required": ["pattern"],
        },
    },
]

def call_tool(name: str, args: dict) -> str:
    if name == "fs_read":
        p = safe_path(args["path"])
        lines = p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
        off = args.get("offset", 0)
        lim = args.get("limit", len(lines))
        return "\n".join(lines[off:off + lim])
    if name == "fs_write":
        p = safe_path(args["path"])
        p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        mode = "a" if args.get("append") else "w"
        with p.open(mode, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write(args["content"])
        return f"wrote {len(args['content'])} chars to {p}"
    if name == "fs_list":
        p = safe_path(args.get("path", "."))
        return "\n".join(sorted(x.name for x in p.iterdir()))
    if name == "fs_search":
        p = safe_path(args.get("path", "."))
        rx = re.compile(args["pattern"])
        hits, cap = [], args.get("max_results", 50)
        for f in p.rglob("*"):
            if not f.is_file():
                continue
            try:
                for i, line in enumerate(f.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines(), 1):
                    if rx.search(line):
                        hits.append(f"{f.relative_to(BASE)}:{i}: {line}")
                        if len(hits) >= cap:
                            return "\n".join(hits)
            except (UnicodeDecodeError, OSError):
                continue
        return "\n".join(hits)
    raise ValueError(f"unknown tool: {name}")

def handle(req: dict) -> dict:
    method = req.get("method")
    if method == "initialize":
        return {"protocolVersion": "2024-11-05", "capabilities": {"tools": {}},
                "serverInfo": {"name": "mini-fs", "version": "0.1.0"}}
    if method == "tools/list":
        return {"tools": TOOLS}
    if method == "tools/call":
        params = req.get("params", {})
        result = call_tool(params["name"], params.get("arguments", {}))
        return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": result}]}
    return {"error": {"code": -32601, "message": "method not found"}}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for line in sys.stdin:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line:
            continue
        try:
            resp = handle(json.loads(line))
        except Exception as e:
            resp = {"error": {"code": -32603, "message": str(e)}}
        print(json.dumps(resp), flush=True)

Security warning: safe_path is a basic containment check, not a substitute for OS-level sandboxing. fs_write and fs_search operate on the real filesystem. Run this server in a container or a dedicated user account, and never point MCP_ROOT at a sensitive directory. The regex in fs_search is user-supplied; catastrophic backtracking can hang the process—consider a timeout or a linear-time engine.

2. Measuring the savings 

import json, tiktoken
from pathlib import Path

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

def schema_tokens(tools_path: str) -> int:
    tools = json.loads(Path(tools_path).read_text())
    return len(enc.encode(json.dumps(tools)))

print("before:", schema_tokens("old_tools.json"))
print("after :", schema_tokens("new_tools.json"))

In my run: before: 2,914, after: 612. Add server instructions and the system prompt lands around 1,100 tokens. That's a ~60% reduction in fixed overhead per request.

3. An agent loop with explicit termination

If you wire these tools into an agent, define when it stops. Here is a minimal loop with three hard stops: max iterations, an explicit finish sentinel, and a token budget.

MAX_ITERS = 8
TOKEN_BUDGET = 20_000

def run_agent(user_msg, call_model, tools):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_msg}]
    used = 0
    for _ in range(MAX_ITERS):
        reply = call_model(messages, tools)  # returns {"tool": ..., "args": ...} or {"text": ...}
        used += reply.get("tokens", 0)
        if used > TOKEN_BUDGET:
            return "stopped: token budget exceeded"
        if "text" in reply:
            return reply["text"]
        result = call_tool(reply["tool"], reply["args"])
        messages.append({"role": "tool", "name": reply["tool"], "content": result})
    return "stopped: max iterations reached"

Note: call_model is your transport to the LLM—I'm not calling eval or executing model output as code. Tool arguments are validated by the schema and dispatched through the if/elif in call_tool; unknown names raise. If you extend this, keep that allowlist.

Key Takeaways

  • Tool schemas are a per-request tax. Count them with tiktoken before and after any refactor.
  • Collapse variations into parameters. Three read_file* tools become one fs_read with offset/limit.
  • Use a discovery meta-tool for the long tail. Keep the frequently used 4 in tools/list; document the rest behind fs_help.
  • Shorter descriptions are real savings. Drop marketing prose; keep types and constraints.
  • Measure, don't guess. A 15→4 cut moved my baseline from ~4,800 to ~1,100 tokens.
  • Sandbox file tools. Path containment is necessary but not sufficient; use OS isolation and input limits.

The protocol didn't change—the surface did. Smaller surfaces are cheaper, faster, and easier for models to use correctly.

title: How to keep a RAG knowledge base fresh without re-embedding everything
summary:
Most RAG pipelines I look at are refreshed by brute force: re-crawl the docs site every night, re-chunk everything, re-embed everything, overwrite the index. It works, eventually, but it's wasteful and it hides three bugs a nightly rebuild never fixes.

Below is what actually goes stale, what a full rebuild really costs (less than you'd think in embeddings, more elsewhere), a do-it-yourself content-hash pattern you can drop into any scraper, and how we handle it in MeshArc, the crawler I'm building. The first half needs no sign-up for anything.

What goes wrong when a knowledge base ages

A stale chunk does not announce itself. It still sits close to the query in vector space, so retrieval still ranks it highly and the model still quotes it with confidence. Three failure modes are worth separating:

  1. Stale chunks. The page changed; the index holds the old wording. The assistant recommends a deprecated flag or an old price.
  2. Zombie chunks. The page was deleted, but its vectors were not. Nightly upserts never remove anything, so deleted pages live on indefinitely unless something deletes them on purpose.
  3. Flicker re-embeds. A cookie banner, a "last updated 3 minutes ago" line or a rotating testimonial makes every page look modified on every run, so a "changed pages only" pipeline quietly turns back into a full rebuild.

There is a fourth, nastier one: the blocked crawl that deletes your index. If the site rate-limits you halfway through a run and your pipeline treats "not seen this run" as "removed", you wipe half the knowledge base. Any deletion logic needs a guard against partial runs.

What a full nightly rebuild costs

Here is the arithmetic for a mid-sized documentation site. The assumptions are ours and stated so you can swap in your own:

  • 2,000 pages, averaging 1,200 words each.
  • Chunks of about 350 words with a 40-word overlap, which gives roughly 4 chunks per page and 8,000 chunks in all.
  • About 1.3 tokens per English word.
  • OpenAI text-embedding-3-small at $0.02 per million input tokens (OpenAI's model page, checked on 23 October 2026).

That is roughly 2.8 million embedded words, or 3.7 million tokens, per full rebuild: about $0.07. Thirty nights is about $2.20 a month.

So, to be fair to the brute-force approach: with a small embedding model, the embedding bill is not what hurts. A larger model, a bigger corpus or a hosted embedding service with per-request pricing changes that, but the real costs of rebuilding everything are usually elsewhere:

  • Fetching. 2,000 pages × 30 nights is 60,000 page reads a month, every one of which can be blocked, rate-limited or billed.
  • Index writes. 8,000 chunk upserts a night, most of them writing identical vectors over identical vectors. Managed vector databases tend to price writes, and self-hosted ones still pay for them in compaction and I/O.
  • Correctness. A rebuild that overwrites by ID still leaves zombies behind, and a rebuild that drops and recreates the index has a window in which the assistant answers from nothing.

The fix for all of these is the same: find out what changed, and touch only that.

The do-it-yourself version: hash, compare, delete deliberately

You do not need any particular vendor for this. The pattern is:

  1. Normalise each page's text (strip boilerplate, collapse whitespace) and hash it.
  2. Compare against the hash you stored last time.
  3. Re-chunk and re-embed only pages whose hash moved; give every chunk an ID that starts with the page URL.
  4. Before adding a changed page's new chunks, delete all of its old ones. The chunk count can shrink, so overwriting by ID is not enough.
  5. Delete pages that have disappeared, but only if the run reached most of the site. 
import hashlib, json, re
from pathlib import Path

STATE = Path("hashes.json")

def normalise(text: str) -> str:
    text = re.sub(r"Last updated[^\n]*", "", text)   # add your own volatile lines
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()

def plan_refresh(pages: dict[str, str], expected_urls: int):
    """pages: {url: markdown} from this run. Returns what to embed and delete."""
    old = json.loads(STATE.read_text()) if STATE.exists() else {}
    new = {u: hashlib.sha256(normalise(t).encode()).hexdigest() for u, t in pages.items()}

    changed = [u for u, h in new.items() if old.get(u) != h]
    removed = [u for u in old if u not in new]

    # Guard: a run that saw under 90% of the site must not delete anything.
    if len(pages) < 0.9 * expected_urls:
        removed = []
        new = {**old, **new}          # keep unseen pages' hashes for next time

    STATE.write_text(json.dumps(new))
    return changed, removed

# changed -> delete chunks with IDs starting f"{url}#", then embed and add new chunks
# removed -> delete chunks with IDs starting f"{url}#"

Two honest caveats. First, this still fetches every page every night to compute the hashes; it saves embedding and index writes, not crawling. Second, the normalise function is where the work lives. Every site has its own flicker, and you will be adding regexes for months.

title: How to find verified Alibaba suppliers with a low MOQ in bulk (and what a first order really costs)
summary:
I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify ($1.50 per 1,000 products) with a free trial credit.

If you have ever sourced on Alibaba, you know the loop: search "yoga mat", open 40 tabs, check each one for the Verified badge, scroll to find the MOQ, squint at "US $7.50-$14.00", then try to remember which supplier was 3 years old and which was 18. Alibaba's own filters help, but they only show you one page at a time and you can't sort by "how much cash do I need to place a first order".

This post shows how to get that whole table at once: every listing for a keyword with its MOQ, price ladder, Verified / Trade Assurance status, supplier age, rating and the inspection company behind the badge. First the no-code way (a form and a CSV), then a short Python script. All numbers below come from a real run of Alibaba Scraper on 24 Sep 2026: 75 listings each for "bluetooth earbuds", "yoga mat", "custom tote bags" and "led strip lights".

What "verified" actually means on Alibaba

Three different badges get mixed up:

  • Verified supplier: the company was inspected on site by a third party. The scraper returns who did it in supplierVerifiedBy. In our run that was always one of SGS, TÜV Rheinland or Intertek.
  • Trade Assurance: Alibaba's payment protection on the order. Almost everyone has it (73 of 75 earbud listings, 75 of 75 yoga mats), so it doesn't separate anyone.
  • Gold supplier: a paid membership. All 300 listings in our run had it, so it says nothing either.

The badge that filters is Verified: 32 of 75 earbud listings, 60 of 75 yoga mats, 61 of 75 tote bags, 62 of 75 LED strips. Combine it with supplier age and rating and the list shrinks fast:

Keyword Listings Unique suppliers Verified Verified + MOQ ≤ 50 ...and 5+ years, rating 4.5+
bluetooth earbuds 75 71 32 24 19
yoga mat 75 29 60 43 10
custom tote bags 75 48 61 13 3
led strip lights 75 56 62 46 29

Two things stand out. Yoga mat results come from only 29 suppliers for 75 listings, so the same factories repeat a lot (dedupe by supplier before you contact anyone). And custom tote bags are a high-MOQ category: the median MOQ was 100 pieces, so only 3 suppliers pass a strict low-MOQ filter.

The number Alibaba doesn't show: cash for a first order

A listing's MOQ times the unit price at that quantity is the smallest order you can place. For yoga mats, the median listing needs $377 for a first order (median MOQ 50 at the first price tier). For earbuds it's $99, for LED strips $115. That's the column I sort a shortlist by when testing a product.

Here are the cheapest first orders among verified, 5+ year, 4.5+ rated yoga mat suppliers in that run (one row per supplier):

Arch Oval Curve Shaped Mat 1 piece $14.00 $14.00 Nantong Vigor Sport Goods 8 4.9 TÜV Rheinland
LEECORK Organic Cork TPE Yoga Mat 12 pieces $8.51 $102.12 Xi'an Leecork 18 4.9 SGS
Micogo Anti Slip Custom Logo Mat 12 pieces $13.80 $165.60 Ningbo Winz Sports Goods 8 4.7 TÜV Rheinland
Natural Rubber PU Leather Mat 50 pieces $10.00 $500.00 Dongguan Tongtianxia Rubber 19 4.8 SGS

That is five inspected, established factories you can order samples from for under $500 total, found in one run instead of an afternoon of tabs.

Option 1: no code (form in, spreadsheet out)

  1. Open the actor page and click Try for free (new Apify accounts get a monthly free credit, which covers a few thousand products).
  2. In Search terms, add your keywords, one per line: yoga mat, cork yoga mat, tpe yoga mat. Narrow variants matter because Alibaba serves about 960 products per keyword.
  3. Under Filters, tick Verified suppliers only, set Max MOQ (for example 50) and optionally a Supplier country (CN, IN, VN, TR...).
  4. Set Max results per search to 200 and click Start. 1,000 products take about 20 seconds.
  5. In the Output tab, download CSV or Excel and open it in Google Sheets or Excel.

In the sheet, keep these columns and sort by minOrderValue (the first-order cash, computed for you in the current version): title, moq, moqUnit, priceAtMoq, minOrderValue, supplierName, supplierYears, supplierRating, supplierVerifiedBy, responseRate, contactSupplierUrl. The last one opens Alibaba's own contact form for that product, so outreach stays on Alibaba with Trade Assurance.

import csv

run = client.actor("rel8ble/alibaba-product-search-scraper").call(run_input={
    "searchTerms": ["yoga mat", "cork yoga mat", "tpe yoga mat"],
    "maxResultsPerSearch": 200,
    "verifiedSuppliersOnly": True,
    "maxMoq": 50,
    "includeAds": False,
})

    tiers = p.get("priceTiers") or []

title: Extracting invoice fields with validation: what auto-posts and what goes to a human
summary:
Pulling an invoice number or a total out of text is the easy half of the job. The useful half is deciding, for every field of every document, whether it goes straight into the accounting system or lands on a person's desk. Here is how a small demo handles it. Everything below is test data from a public synthetic dataset, not a client result.

What the demo does

Input: the OCR text of an invoice. Output: invoice number, date, IBAN and gross total, each with a confidence. Fields with low confidence are routed to a human instead of being posted.

The data is mychen76/invoices-and-receipts_ocr_v1: OCR text plus ground-truth fields. The invoices are synthetic with a fixed layout, and only the invoice-type documents are used (484 of about 2,200; the rest are receipts with a different schema).

Candidates first, then a ranker

For each field the code generates candidates with patterns, then a small logistic regression picks the right one using context: the words around the candidate, its position, its format. This matters most for the total, because an invoice contains many amounts (net, tax, line items, gross) and "the biggest number" is not the answer.

Validation beats confidence for IBANs

For IBANs the demo does not trust a score at all. It validates the ISO 13616 checksum. If OCR confused one character (S for 5, O for 0, a dropped or doubled character) and exactly one repair makes the checksum pass, it applies the repair. If no unique valid value exists, the field goes to a human.

def iban_ok(s: str) -> bool:
    s = s.replace(" ", "").upper()
    rearranged = s[4:] + s[:4]
    digits = "".join(str(int(c, 36)) for c in rearranged)
    return int(digits) % 97 == 1

A checksum is a hard gate a model cannot talk its way past.

Results on 74 held-out documents (test data)

Field Docs scored Accuracy when automated Automated share
Invoice number 74 100% 97.3%
Invoice date 74 100% 100%
IBAN 56 100% 100%
Gross total 74 98.6% 100%

96.4% of clean documents were fully automated (all four fields), and 98.2% of those had every field correct. Thresholds were tuned on a validation split for a 98% target; the held-out set was used for reporting only.

Honest caveats

  • 74 documents with a fixed synthetic layout is a small, friendly test. Real, varied invoices will score lower, and a pilot starts by measuring on the client's own sample.
  • In 18 of the 74 documents the dataset's IBAN label itself fails the checksum while the OCR text passes it, so the label is corrupted. Those are excluded from the IBAN score and counted separately in results.json. Check your ground truth before blaming the model.
  • The input is OCR text. Turning scans and PDFs into that text is a separate, replaceable step.

Takeaways

  1. Decide per field what is allowed to auto-post, with a number as the bar.
  2. Use deterministic validation (checksums, date ranges, sum checks) wherever it exists.
  3. Route what you cannot validate to a human, and make that route cheap.
  4. Audit your labels before you measure.

title: Reading Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby job boards from their public JSON endpoints
summary:
AI disclosure: this post was written with AI assistance (drafting and editing). I ran every request and code sample below myself on October 28, 2026 and checked the output. Select "AI-Assisted" in the DEV editor before publishing.

If you want a list of open jobs at a set of companies, you usually do not need a headless browser. Most tech companies host their career page on an applicant tracking system (ATS), and three of the most common ones, Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby, expose the same postings their career pages render as plain JSON. No API key, no login.

This post covers the three endpoints, the fields worth keeping, and a small reader that turns all three into one shape.

1. Find the board name

The board name is in the career page URL:

ATS Career page looks like Board name
Greenhouse boards.greenhouse.io/airbnb or job-boards.greenhouse.io/airbnb airbnb
Lever jobs.lever.co/spotify spotify
Ashby jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp ramp

If a company uses its own domain, view the page source and search for greenhouse, lever.co or ashbyhq. The embed script or the apply links usually give it away.

2. The endpoints

Greenhouse (Job Board API, docs):

GET https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{board}/jobs?content=true

Returns {"jobs": [...], "meta": {"total": N}}. Each job has id, title, location.name, absolute_url, updated_at, first_published and, with content=true, an HTML-escaped description in content. Drop content=true if you only need titles; the response gets much smaller.

Lever (Postings API, docs):

GET https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{site}?mode=json

Returns a bare JSON array. Useful fields: id, text (the title), categories.location, categories.team, categories.commitment, workplaceType, hostedUrl, createdAt (epoch milliseconds). Companies on Lever's EU instance use api.eu.lever.co instead. An unknown site returns {"ok": false, "error": "Document not found"} with a 404, so check for a list before iterating.

Ashby (public job posting API, docs):

GET https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{board}?includeCompensation=true

Returns {"jobs": [...]}. Fields: id, title, department, team, location, secondaryLocations, isRemote, workplaceType, employmentType, publishedAt, jobUrl, applyUrl. With includeCompensation=true, many jobs carry compensation.compensationTierSummary, a ready-to-display string such as $211.4K – $290.6K • Offers Equity. Salary data is the main reason I reach for Ashby boards first.

3. One reader for all three

Standard library only:

import json
import urllib.request

UA = {"User-Agent": "job-board-reader/1.0 (+you@example.com)"}


def get_json(url):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers=UA)
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
        return json.load(r)


def greenhouse(board):
    data = get_json(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{board}/jobs?content=true")
    for j in data["jobs"]:
        yield {
            "source": "greenhouse", "id": str(j["id"]), "title": j["title"],
            "location": (j.get("location") or {}).get("name"),
            "posted": j.get("first_published") or j.get("updated_at"),
            "url": j["absolute_url"],
        }


def lever(site):
    for j in get_json(f"https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{site}?mode=json"):
        cats = j.get("categories") or {}
        yield {
            "source": "lever", "id": j["id"], "title": j["text"],
            "location": cats.get("location"),
            "posted": j.get("createdAt"),  # epoch milliseconds
            "url": j["hostedUrl"],
        }


def ashby(board):
    data = get_json(f"https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{board}?includeCompensation=true")
    for j in data["jobs"]:
        yield {
            "source": "ashby", "id": j["id"], "title": j["title"],
            "location": j.get("location"),
            "posted": j.get("publishedAt"),
            "url": j["jobUrl"],
        }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    jobs = [*greenhouse("airbnb"), *lever("spotify"), *ashby("ramp")]
    print(len(jobs), "jobs")

When I ran it, it printed 456 jobs (195 Greenhouse, 89 Lever, 172 Ashby), in under a second end to end.

4. Things that bite

  • Dates come in three formats. Greenhouse uses ISO 8601 with a local offset, Ashby uses ISO 8601 in UTC, and Lever uses epoch milliseconds. Normalize before you sort or filter by "posted in the last N days".
  • Greenhouse updated_at is not the posting date. It changes when a recruiter edits the job. Prefer first_published when it is present.
  • Locations are free text. "Remote - USA", "United States" and "New York, NY (HQ)" all appear. Ashby's isRemote and Lever's workplaceType are more reliable than parsing strings.
  • IDs are only unique per ATS. Prefix them (ashby:) before you dedupe across sources.
  • Descriptions are HTML. Greenhouse's is HTML-escaped HTML, so unescape first, then strip tags.
  • Detecting new jobs is just a set difference: store the prefixed IDs you have seen, and on the next run keep only IDs you have not seen.

5. Be a polite client

These endpoints exist so career pages can render, and that is the reason they are open. Treat them that way:

  • Send a descriptive User-Agent with a contact address.
  • Check robots.txt. On the day I wrote this, api.lever.co/robots.txt allowed everything with Crawl-delay: 1, and boards-api.greenhouse.io/robots.txt disallowed only /embed/.
  • One request per board is enough. Each endpoint returns the whole board, so polling once or twice a day covers almost every use case.
  • Only collect what the company has already published. Do not try to reach application data or anything behind a login.

Workday career sites are the big platform missing from this list. They also serve JSON, but through a per-tenant POST endpoint with pagination and facets, which deserves a post of its own.

Workday career sites are the big platform missing from this list. They also serve JSON, but through a per-tenant POST endpoint with pagination and facets, which deserves a post of its own.
